title: Active-active backpressure choreography for token-aware streaming
creator: Aisha Thompson
body:
Summary:
Implement an active-active traffic controller that applies coordinated backpressure across edge gateways to preserve SLOs for tail latency and token-preservation for streaming sessions. The goal is to enable multi-region active-active operation while avoiding session truncation and spurious reconnects when a region becomes degraded or saturated. This ticket covers design, prototype, and a canary rollout for the controller plus instrumentation and runbook updates.

Context and motivation:
- We operate active-active gateways in multiple regions for hosted API traffic. When a region experiences capacity pressure (GPU saturation, network congestion, or a transient control-plane slowdown), naively shifting traffic causes either large latency tails (increasing 99th pct) or abrupt session termination for streaming clients.
- Existing circuit-breaker behavior is coarse: open/closed per endpoint and often results in early hard-cut evictions. Load-shedding at gateway level exists but lacks session-awareness and token preservation semantics.
- SLOs: generation latency P95 < 250ms, P99 < 1200ms for small payloads; streaming continuity SLO: 99.9% sessions not interrupted mid-stream due to failover.

Design overview:
- "Backpressure Choreography" is a coordinated, per-session, token-aware flow-control layer deployed at edge gateways and the regional traffic router. Key parts:
  1) Local hydraulic governor: each gateway exposes a lightweight pressure signal (pressurescore) computed from readouts (GPU queue depth, KV cache hit tail, scheduler backlog, network egress latency). Pressurescore is mapped to graded shedding actions rather than binary rejects.
  2) Session escrow and token windows: for long-running streaming sessions, we maintain a small ephemeral session escrow (session metadata & last N tokens) replicated to a warm standby in another region. The controller enforces a token-preservation window (configurable, default 64 tokens) to ensure relay continuity during soft shifts.
  3) Coordinated soft-shift protocol: when pressurescore crosses thresholds, the ingress controller negotiates a soft-shift with downstream gateways. Soft-shift transitions are staged in three phases: attenuate (gradual percentage bleed), escrow-warmup (ensure standby snapshot is fresh), and redirect (move new session steering).
  4) Circuit-tiering: extend existing circuit breakers with a two-axis (latency degradation vs error spike) tier model. Tier-1 triggers graded shedding; Tier-2 triggers session anchor migration; Tier-3 triggers full re-route.
  5) Telemetry + decision audit trail: every choreography decision emits a compact event (controller_id, pressurescore, action, sessions_affected, token_window) to the telemetry pipeline for SLO correlation and retrospective analysis.

Trade-offs and rationale:
- Why graded shedding vs binary rejects: preserves UX for most sessions, reduces churn from reconnects, and provides predictable SLO behavior by limiting the rate of affected requests.
- Why token-window escrow: full session replication (entire token history & KV content) is expensive and increases synchronous write pressure. We instead store a small token window and last model KV checkpoint; in practice this preserves streaming continuity for the majority of real-world sessions.
- Additional cost: standby warm sessions will raise cross-region replication traffic slightly (~1–2% overall). We estimate incremental infra cost of ~0.7% on Dedicated fleet for indexing and ephemeral storage.

Acceptance criteria:
- Controller prototype deployed to staging with synthetic traffic generator (see sim harness link).
- Synthetic failure scenarios (GPU backlog spike, network egress loss, control-plane timeout) produce: P99 latency increase capped at +20% compared to baseline and session interruption rate < 0.1% for streaming tests across 10k sessions.
- Telemetry events emitted for every decision; Dashboard (SLO controller view) created and linked.
- Canary rollout plan and automations for rollback in Console.

Implementation plan:
1) Instrumentation and pressurescore: implement pressurescore computation in runtime agent (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/6721).
2) Session escrow API: add lightweight escrow service and APIs (design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Token+Window+Escrow+Design).
3) Controller and coordinator: new microservice "edge-backpressure-controller" with leader election per-region, gRPC interface to gateways.
4) Circuit-tier extension: update policy engine to support tiered thresholds and mapping to graded actions.
5) Telemetry and dashboard: add decision events to event pipeline and Grafana dashboard (grafana/dashboard/edge-backpressure.json).
6) Simulations and chaos tests: evolve sim harness (https://github.com/redwood-inference/sim-harness/compare/backpressure) to run multi-region degraded scenarios.
7) Canary rollout: stage -> us-west-2 -> eu-west-1 with 1% traffic -> 5% -> 25% -> full. Automated rollback on SLO breach.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for pressurescore mapping and action selection.
- Integration tests validating escrow snapshot/restore within token window limits.
- Load tests against dedicated pool replicating 25k concurrent streaming sessions.
- Chaos scenarios: induce staggered GPU OOMs, saturate scheduler, drop inter-region network for 30s, validate session-preservation and SLOs.

Rollout and runbook notes:
- Canary gating: must have <2x baseline error rate and P99 increase < 1.5x at 5% traffic before advancing.
- Runbook highlights: if controller abnormal state appears (stuck in attenuate for >90s), emergency step is to engage manual egress-limit in Console and enable conservative circuit-tier.
- Ops pager: on-call will receive anomaly alerts for pressurescore excursion >0.85 for >60s or session-interruption rate >0.05%.

Open questions and considerations:
- Eviction fairness: how to ensure fair shedding across customers with mixed quotas and enterprise tenants? Propose per-tenant weight and emergency premium-protect flag.
- Edge-case: frequent short sessions may not have meaningful token windows; need to prioritize these for graceful degradation.
- Compliance: cross-region session escrow touches customer data in transient form; confirm encryption-at-rest and KMS policies for ephemeral objects.

References and artefacts:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Token+Window+Escrow+Design
- Runtime PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/6721
- Sim harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sim-harness/tree/backpressure
- Draft dashboard: grafana/redwood/edge-backpressure-controller

Next steps (short-term):
- Deliver pressurescore prototype (owner: Diego) and initial unit tests by 2026-03-08.
- Implement escrow API skeleton and run integration smoke tests by 2026-03-18.
- Kick off chaos matrix scenarios with SRE and evaluate results week of 2026-03-23.

acceptance_criteria: Pressurescore emitted and visible in telemetry for each gateway
Controller enacts graded shedding without session truncation for 99.9% of streaming sessions in synthetic test
Canary pipeline and rollback automated in Console
Documentation and runbook created and reviewed by SRE and Security
risks: Transient data exposure via cross-region escrow (mitigated by KMS + TTL)
Increased operational cost from warm-standby session artifacts
Unintended feedback loops between gateways if thresholds miscalibrated
notes: Keep incremental resource usage dashboards visible during canary (cost delta and egress). Iterate thresholds conservatively; prefer slightly higher latency to client-visible session truncation.
